companies.name: Broadcom
companies.theme: Custom AI accelerators + Ethernet/networking + AI connectivity
companies.thesis: Broadcom is one of the cleanest non-GPU AI infrastructure beneficiaries because custom accelerators and networking are scaling together. Q3 FY26 revenue reached $29.6B and management's multi-year AI semiconductor outlook implies a much larger 2027-28 revenue base. The evidence raises demand conviction, but customer concentration and valuation still require entry discipline.
companies.catalysts: Custom XPU ramps, Ethernet/networking attach, hyperscaler deployments, AI semiconductor revenue conversion and FCF.
companies.risks: Customer concentration, execution against unusually large forward forecasts, AI-capex slowdown and multiple compression under high real yields.

companies.name: Micron Technology
companies.thesis: Memory is moving from commodity component toward architectural bottleneck. HBM, DDR5, NAND, CXL and tighter memory-compute integration benefit Micron's broad portfolio, while constrained cleanroom/wafer capacity supports pricing. The long-term thesis is stronger, but memory remains cyclical and supply additions can eventually reverse scarcity.
companies.catalysts: HBM ramps, DRAM/NAND pricing, AI server memory content, 3D/tightly-coupled architecture progress and earnings guidance.
companies.risks: Memory-cycle reversal, capex/supply response, Samsung/SK hynix competition, execution and high expectations.

companies.name: Credo Technology Group
companies.theme: High-speed connectivity + optical DSP + memory fanout
companies.thesis: Credo is a direct beneficiary of the data-movement bottleneck. Q1 FY27 revenue was $479M, up 114.7% YoY, with Q2 guidance of $525-535M. Its copper, optical and OmniConnect products address the bandwidth and memory-fanout problems created by larger AI systems.
companies.catalysts: Optical/interconnect growth, scale-out networking, OmniConnect adoption, customer diversification and margin durability.
companies.risks: Customer concentration, premium valuation, rapid competitive change and AI-capex concentration.

companies.name: Dell Technologies
companies.thesis: Dell provides hard evidence that funded AI demand is enormous: Q2 AI orders were $60.9B, AI server revenue $16.4B and backlog $95B. The opportunity is real, but lower hardware margins, supply constraints and working-capital intensity make Dell a different quality profile from semiconductor or electrical bottleneck suppliers.
companies.catalysts: Backlog conversion, AI server shipments, enterprise adoption, supply normalization and margin/FCF conversion.
companies.risks: Low-margin mix, component constraints, working-capital swings, customer concentration and normalization after the backlog surge.

companies.name: Hewlett Packard Enterprise
companies.thesis: HPE's Q3 FY26 results confirm broad AI infrastructure demand: Cloud & AI revenue reached $9.0B, server revenue $6.8B and data-center networking $382M. Management also describes DDR5, DDR4 and NAND as constrained and has signed multi-year supply agreements, reinforcing the memory-scarcity thesis. Juniper integration and inventory intensity keep it below the highest-quality picks.
companies.catalysts: Cloud/AI growth, networking mix, Juniper synergies, memory supply security, FCF recovery and margin expansion.
companies.risks: Large inventory build, supply costs, integration execution, hardware cyclicality and lower-margin AI server mix.

companies.name: Snowflake
companies.thesis: Snowflake confirms that AI demand is reaching the application/data layer rather than stopping at infrastructure. Q2 FY27 product revenue was $1.49B, up 37%, with $9.0B RPO up 30% and management citing accelerating AI usage. Strong execution is offset by high-duration valuation risk while long yields remain elevated.
companies.catalysts: Product-revenue acceleration, AI workload consumption, RPO conversion, margin/FCF leverage and yield relief.
companies.risks: Valuation compression, cloud competition, consumption volatility and slower enterprise spending.
